scenes.visual: Title card: Recognize and Respond: Innate Immunity.

scenes.tts: Long before your body can make new antibodies against a microbe, it is already defending itself. Innate immunity is the set of defenses an organism has before it meets a particular microbe. Barriers keep many microbes out. For the ones that get in, ready-made receptors recognize whole classes of microbial molecules, and signs of damage. That recognition sets off a fast, coordinated response, inflammation, which brings eating cells and blood proteins to the site.
scenes.visual: A tissue surface: a barrier bar turns most microbes away; one gets in; a receptor on a resident cell lights up on contact; arrows show eating cells and blood proteins converging on the spot.

scenes.tts: In a mammal, resident cells such as macrophages carry pattern-recognition receptors. One, T L R four, recognizes lipopolysaccharide, a molecule from the outer membrane of many bacteria. Sensing switches on inflammatory genes. Mediators such as histamine widen small vessels and loosen their lining. Fluid and plasma proteins, complement among them, leak into the tissue. Neutrophils squeeze out of the vessel, and monocytes follow. Macrophages clear microbes and debris, and the tissue rebuilds.

scenes.tts: Barriers come first. Skin's outer layer is dead, tightly packed cells. In airways, mucus traps microbes, and cilia carry it out. Stomach acid kills many swallowed microbes. Lining cells release antimicrobial peptides, and harmless resident microbes take the space a newcomer would need.
scenes.visual: Four quick panels: dead packed skin cells; airway mucus and cilia moving it up and out; stomach acid; lining cells releasing antimicrobial peptides beside resident microbes filling the space.

scenes.tts: A microbe that gets through meets a phagocyte, a cell that engulfs particles. Lysosomes fuse with the bubble that holds it and usually kill it. The evidence came from a transparent water flea. Elie Metchnikoff watched its blood cells swallow invading yeast spores. Where the cells destroyed the spores, the infection stopped. Where spores grew, the flea died.
scenes.visual: A phagocyte engulfs a microbe; lysosomes fuse with the bubble; then the transparent flea: blood cells engulf needle-shaped spores (flea intact) beside a second flea filled with budding yeast (flea dies).

scenes.tts: Complement is a set of proteins in blood plasma. When C three is cut, its large piece, C three b, sticks to a microbe and marks it for eating. The small pieces, C three a and, a step later, C five a, drift away and promote inflammation. Later pieces can punch holes in susceptible microbes.

scenes.tts: Against viruses, interferons from infected cells put nearby cells into an antiviral state. Natural killer cells kill infected or abnormal cells. A cell that has lost a normal surface protein, M H C class one, removes a brake on them.

scenes.visual: Interferon passes from an infected cell to a neighbour, which turns a protected colour; an NK cell passes a cell showing MHC class I, then removes a cell that has lost it.

scenes.tts: Flies make no antibodies, yet flies and plants each recognize microbes with their own receptors. Innate immunity does not build new receptors in each B or T cell, so it lacks their receptor-based memory. What it gives is speed: keep microbes out, recognize the ones that get in, and gather the defenses that clear them.
scenes.visual: A fly, a plant leaf and a mouse side by side, each with its own receptor icon; then a three-step strip: barrier, receptor, gathered defenders clearing microbes.
